# Chapt. 1 -- The Reproducibility Crisis {#chap1}
## Goal

In this chapter, we engage in group activities and literature reading to **explore the concept of reproducible science**, including its challenges, benefits, and practical implementation in research. Overall, this chapter aims to provide a broader understanding of reproducible science and the context that underpins the material covered throughout the course.

The chapter is subdivided into two parts:

- [PART A:](#WhatRepSci) What is Reproducible Science?
- [PART B:](#WhatFacBreakRep) What Factors Break Reproducibility?

## Learning Outcomes

- Understand the definitions of reproducibility and replicability in scientific research
- Identify the importance of reproducible science for research integrity and advancements
- Recognize the challenges to achieving reproducibility and potential solutions
- Engage with practical tools and strategies to promote reproducible research practices 

## Online Resources {#OnlineResChap1}

This list of online resources supports our group activities:

- [Reproducibility and Replicability in Science](https://doi.org/10.17226/25303) - A report published by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine.
- [Retraction Watch](https://retractionwatch.com/) - Tracking retractions as a window into the scientific process.
- [PubPeer](https://pubpeer.com/) - An online journal club where researchers are posting comments on articles.
- [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/) - This database comprises more than 39 million citations for biomedical literature from MEDLINE, life science journals, and online books. Citations may include links to full text content from PubMed Central and publisher web sites.
- [RESCIENCE C](http://rescience.github.io/) - Reproducible Science is good. Replicated Science is better.
- [Peer Review Week](https://peerreviewweek.net/index.php) - Peer Review Week is a community-led yearly global virtual event celebrating the essential role that peer review plays in maintaining research quality. The event brings together individuals, institutions, and organizations committed to sharing the central message that quality peer review in whatever shape or form it may take is critical to scholarly communication.
- [Research Integrity and Peer Review](https://researchintegrityjournal.biomedcentral.com/) - An international, open access, peer reviewed journal that encompasses all aspects of integrity in research publication, including peer review, study reporting, and research and publication ethics.
- [Tools such as ChatGPT threaten transparent science; here are our ground rules for their use](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-023-00191-1) - A *Nature* editorial discussing the inclusion of AI in research articles.

## What is Reproducible Science? {#WhatRepSci}

To investigate this question, **students engage in self-reflection and group activities designed to explore the meaning of reproducible science and its implementation in research** and scientific publications.

**Disclaimer:** The instructor has provided definitions and other supporting materials (in collapsible boxes) throughout this section. However, students are advised not to read these materials in advance, in order to complete the exercises sincerely and derive the greatest benefit from the experience.  

### Class Outline

The structure of this class, held over two sessions, is as follows:

1. [Introduction and Definitions](#IntroDef) <span style="color:dimgray;">(30 minutes)</span>
2. [Case Studies and Challenges](#CaseStudies) <span style="color:dimgray;">(80 minutes over two sessions)</span>
3. [Best Practices and Open Science Tools](#BestPract) <span style="color:dimgray;">(20 minutes)</span>
4. [Wrap-up and Future Directions](#WrapUp) <span style="color:dimgray;">(10 minutes)</span>

The first two sections will be covered during Session 1, while the remaining sections will be addressed in Session 2.  
Please ensure that you have identified the reproducibility challenges in your assigned publication (see [Case Studies and Challenges](#CaseStudies)) prior to attending the second session. 

### Introduction and Definitions {#IntroDef}

#### ✍️ Individual Self-Reflection <span style="color:dimgray;">(5 minutes)</span>

Students reflect on what **“reproducible science”** means to them and write down a personal definition.

---

#### 🤝 Group Sharing and Discussion <span style="color:dimgray;">(15 minutes)</span>

- Form small groups (2-3 students)
- Small groups share and compare their definitions
- Each group presents insights to the class to foster open discussion

---

#### 📘 Formal Definitions <span style="color:dimgray;">(10 minutes)</span>

Standard definitions are introduced to clarify the distinction between **reproducibility** and **replicability**.  
Students are invited to relate them to their own research experience.

<details>
<summary><b>📌 What is Reproducible Science?</b></summary>

Reproducible science means **achieving the same findings** using the **original data, methods, and code**.

**Key elements:**

- **Transparency** – Open access to data, code, and methods.
- **Documentation** – Clear steps and research design explanation.
- **Data Availability** – Raw data is publicly available.
- **Code Availability** – Scripts are shared and well-commented.
- **Standardized Practices** – Use of trusted tools and workflows.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🔄 Reproduction vs. Replication</b></summary>

**Reproduction** = Running the same code on the same data to verify results (like software testing for an entire study).  
**Replication** = Repeating the study with **intentional variations** (e.g., different species, software, or parameters) to test if conclusions hold.

- **Reproduction** confirms that the research is **traceable** and correctly recorded.
- **Replication** tests **what aspects of a study matter** for the results to hold.

<blockquote><b>Key insight:</b> Replication is most useful <i>after</i> reproduction is verified.</blockquote>

<br>

<b>💭 Think about it:</b> Can you think of examples of scientific studies, methods, or protocols where replication would be particularly important? What would you learn by repeating them with intentional variations?

</details>

### Case Studies and Challenges {#CaseStudies}

#### 👥 Group Work Activity <span style="color:dimgray;">(50 minutes)</span>

Each group is given a real-world **publication that illustrates challenges to reproducibility**, such as:

- 🔒 **Lack of data/code sharing**  
  Data and code are not made available, preventing verification and reuse.
- 🧩 **Incomplete methodological detail**  
  Missing or vague descriptions of protocols, tools, or parameters hinder reproducibility.
- 📉 **Poor statistical practices**  
  Misuse or misunderstanding of statistical tests can lead to invalid conclusions.
- 🎯 **Publication bias**  
  Preference for positive or novel results skews the scientific record and limits replication efforts.
- 🤖 **Unclear or unvalidated use of AI tools**  
  Use of AI (e.g., large language models, predictive algorithms) without documenting models, prompts, parameters, or validation steps reduces transparency and reproducibility.
- 🧪 **Data manipulation or selective reporting**  
  Deliberate or unintentional exclusion, alteration, or cherry-picking of data that misrepresents findings.

#### 📄 Publications Used in This Activity

I assign one of the retracted articles below to each group at the start of the activity. The links are here so that you can find your article again afterwards. The reasons behind each retraction are given at the end of this section --- **work through your article and reach your own conclusions before opening that table.** The articles are also available on our [Google Drive](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1AeoPIzzs4mEUMIhUiACT7TYtUHS9U0Nu?usp=drive_link).

### Best Practices and Open Science Tools {#BestPract}

#### 🧠 Whiteboard Brainstorm <span style="color:dimgray;">(20 minutes)</span>

Working in **2--3 groups, each at a whiteboard**, you will build a two-column list: on the left the **issues** that break reproducibility, and on the right the **best practice or open science tool** that addresses each one.

**Start from the retracted articles you have just worked on.** The case studies in [Case Studies and Challenges](#CaseStudies) and the reasons behind their retractions in Table \@ref(tab:retractionwatch) are your raw material: every entry in the *Reason* column of that table is something that somebody failed to prevent. Begin by asking what would have had to be different for your article never to have been retracted.

**The order matters --- diagnose before you prescribe.**

1. **List the issues first** <span style="color:dimgray;">(~8 minutes)</span>
   What actually went wrong in [your group's article](#CaseStudies), and what does Table \@ref(tab:retractionwatch) say went wrong in the other two? Add anything from the challenge types listed in that section, or from your own research experience. Be specific: *"the raw data were never deposited anywhere"* is workable; *"bad practice"* is not.

2. **Then pair each issue with a solution** <span style="color:dimgray;">(~8 minutes)</span>
   Work along your list and, for every issue, name the practice, habit or tool that would have prevented it. Some issues will attract several solutions; some solutions will fix several issues. Both are worth noticing.

3. **Report back** <span style="color:dimgray;">(~4 minutes)</span>
   Each group walks the class through its board. We will then compare the boards to see which issues everyone found, and which were spotted by only one group.

<blockquote>
💡 <b>One rule:</b> every practice or tool on the right must answer a specific issue on the left. A tool nobody can attach to a problem is a tool you do not yet have a reason to use --- and saying so out loud is a perfectly good contribution.
</blockquote>

### Wrap-up and Future Directions {#WrapUp}

#### 🚀 Key Strategies & Tools <span style="color:dimgray;">(10 minutes)</span>

**With your boards from [the brainstorm](#BestPract) still up**, we now compare them against the short list below and turn the discussion towards your own work.

Three questions guide this last part:

1. **What did we all find?** Which practices appeared on every board, and which on only one? A tool that only one group thought of is usually the one worth talking about.
2. **What is missing from the list below --- and what is missing from your boards?** The list is deliberately short. If your board names something it does not, that is not an error on your part; it is a gap in the list, and I would like to hear it.
3. **What will you actually deploy?** For each strategy, ask whether it belongs in *your* research: could you start using it this semester, does it need a tool you do not yet have, or is it not relevant to the kind of data you work with? Naming one practice you will adopt is worth more than agreeing that all of them are good.

Every item below is developed further in [Chapt. 5 -- Data Management and Reproducible Code](#Chap5), so this is a map of where we are going as much as a summary of where we have been.

Please don't look at the content of the box before we get here!

<details>
    <summary><b> ✅ Strategies and tools for reproducible science</b></summary>
<ul>
  <li><strong>Detailed Protocols:</strong> Importance of clear and precise documentation of all steps leading to data production.</li>
  <li><strong>Lab Notebooks:</strong> For improved documentation and data management.</li>
  <li><strong>Version Control:</strong> Using tools like Git for code and data management.</li>
  <li><strong>Data and Code Repositories:</strong> Platforms like Dryad, Zenodo, and Figshare for sharing research materials.</li>
</ul>
</details>


## What Factors Break Reproducibility? {#WhatFacBreakRep}

### Goal

In Part A, we investigated what reproducible science *is*, and why it fails. In Part B, we ask **which factors break it**, and then we do something about them.

We work from two sources of evidence: the survey of 1,576 researchers published by @Baker_2016, which reports what the scientific community itself blames for irreproducible work, and the report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine [@NAP25303], which sets out what should be done about it.

**The goal of Part B is to turn that evidence into a defence.** By the end of these two sessions your group will have produced one deliverable: a **[reproducibility charter](#draftcharter)** --- a set of standards your research team commits to, each one chosen to block a specific factor known to break reproducible science. It is a short shared document, and if you want to see what a standard actually looks like before we begin, there are [worked examples of charter clauses](#chartertemplate) further down. The diagnosis is where we start; the charter is what we are here to produce.

**Your charter opens by saying what it is for.** Before any of the standards, it states in three lines what your group means by *reproducible science*, and what distinguishes *reproducibility* from *replicability* (the definitions you worked on in [Part A](#IntroDef)). A charter that sets standards without saying what they are for is just a list of rules; those three lines are what the rules are in service of, which is why they sit at the top. Everything below them has to earn its place by serving them.

### Class Outline

This class is run as a single [**group activity**](#FactorsActivity) (writing your group's reproducibility charter) held over two sessions and divided as follows:

1. [Overview of the Group Activity](#FactorsActivity) <span style="color:dimgray;">(10 minutes)</span>
2. [What Do You Remember?](#recall) <span style="color:dimgray;">(10 minutes)</span>

6. [Stress-Test Another Team's Charter](#stresstest) <span style="color:dimgray;">(20 minutes)</span>
7. [Revise and Commit](#commitcharter) <span style="color:dimgray;">(15 minutes)</span>

The first four sections will be covered during Session 1, while the remaining sections will be addressed in Session 2.  
**Each group finishes its draft charter as homework between the two sessions, and adds a short block of definitions at the top**, because Session 2 opens with another group taking it apart (see [Draft Your Charter](#draftcharter)).

Every one of these sections draws on the [**Resources**](#PartBresources) set out below: the two **publications**, the **teaching material**, and the **recommendations** of the National Academies. They are the evidence this class is built on --- you will check your own answers against them in [Review the Resources](#reviewres), and draw on them again for every clause you write into your charter.

### Investigated Questions

We will be investigating the following questions:

- Is there a reproducibility crisis?
- How much published work in your field is reproducible?
- What is the scale of the reproducibility crisis?
- What corrective measures can be implemented?
- What factors contribute to irreproducible research?
- What can be done to mitigate the reproducible crisis?

### 👥 Group Activity: Write Your Lab's Reproducibility Charter {#FactorsActivity}

In this session we cover the material of Part B (the survey evidence of @Baker_2016, the recommendations of @NAP25303, and the [questions listed above](#WhatFacBreakRep)) and then put it to work. You will use it to write something of your own: a **reproducibility charter**.

<blockquote>
📜 <b>Charter</b> <i>(noun)</i> --- a short written document in which a group sets out the standards it binds <i>itself</i> to.
<br><br>
A charter is not advice, and not a summary of good practice. Guidelines describe what researchers in general ought to do; a charter states what <b>this group will always do</b>. Three things follow from that: it is written by the people who will be held to it, each commitment is specific enough that somebody else can tell whether it was kept, and it is public within the group, so colleagues can point to it when it is not.
<br><br>
Research groups, laboratories and consortia write these for exactly this reason --- so that standards survive a deadline, a new student, or a change of principal investigator, instead of living in one person's head.
</blockquote>


#### Why we are doing this

**You already have the evidence you need.** Three things feed this charter, and every clause you write should be traceable to one of them:

1. **What you saw in [Part A](#WhatRepSci).** You examined retracted articles and the reasons behind their retractions (Table \@ref(tab:retractionwatch)). Those are documented failures --- your charter should make them harder to repeat.
2. **What the field reports.** @Baker_2016 tells you which factors researchers themselves blame most often. A charter that ignores the commonest causes is not serious.
3. **What has been recommended.** @NAP25303 sets out what the National Academies concluded should change. You can adopt, adapt or argue with it, but you should know what it says.

**The test for every clause is whether it supports the [scientific process](#scientificprocess)** --- whether it makes it more likely that a claim you publish can be checked, repeated and built on by somebody else. That is what reproducibility is *for*. A standard that is merely tidy, or that only makes your own life easier, is not yet a reproducibility standard.

**And this is not a one-off exercise.** Nearly everything you write today (data management, documentation, reproducible code, version control, deposition, citation) is developed properly later in this course. Your charter is therefore a **map of where we are going**: at the end of the semester you should be able to return to it and find that you now know how to implement what you committed to today, and to judge whether you were ambitious enough.

Work in **two groups of three**. Each group is a research team, and **every member owns one section of the charter**:

| Role | Owns the standards for |
|---|---|
| **Data lead** | How data are generated and recorded: protocols, field and laboratory notes, file naming, storage, backup and metadata |
| **Analysis lead** | Code and statistics: the analysis plan, what is decided before the data are seen, and how an analysis is made re-runnable |
| **Reporting lead** | What leaves the group: what is deposited and when, how results and limitations are reported, and how data, software and sources are cited |

Between them these three cover the whole data life cycle, so nothing in the charter is unowned. **You are responsible for your section and you will be the one defending it**, so choose the role closest to the research you actually do --- or the one furthest from it, if you would rather learn something new.


#### 🧠 What Do You Remember? <span style="color:dimgray;">(10 minutes)</span> {#recall}

**Books closed.** No paper, no slides, no notes, no laptops. You read @Baker_2016 for today, and this is where you find out how much of it stayed with you.

Working as a group, agree on four answers and **write them on a single sheet**:

1. **The scale.** Of the 1,576 researchers surveyed, what share reported a *significant* reproducibility crisis? Give a percentage.
2. **Your own field.** What proportion of published work in your field do you believe is reproducible? This one is not recall --- it is your own judgement, and there is no answer at the back of the book.
3. **The causes.** Which **three factors** did respondents most often blame for irreproducible research? Name them as precisely as you can.
4. **Your shortlist.** From those, a **provisional** list of the three factors you think are most dangerous to *your* research. Provisional because you are about to check your answers, and may want to change your mind.

**Commit to specifics.** "Quite a lot of people" is not an answer; "about 70%" is. Recalling something and getting it wrong fixes the right answer in memory far better than reading it a second time does --- which is the whole point of doing this before you open anything.

<blockquote>
📄 <b>What you take out of this step:</b> one sheet per group, with four answers on it. You will mark it up in <a href="#reviewres">Review the Resources</a>, and your shortlist becomes what the charter has to defend against.
</blockquote>


#### 📖 Review the Resources <span style="color:dimgray;">(10 minutes)</span> {#reviewres}

**Now confirm your answers against the evidence.** You have committed to four answers from memory; this step is where you find out which of them hold up. The PDFs are on our shared Google Drive as well as linked below.

Work **individually, and in silence**. Go to [Resources](#PartBresources) and give each of the three a few minutes:

- the [publications](#PartBpubs) --- check the figures you have just tried to recall, and read around the ones you got wrong;
- the [teaching material](#PartBteaching) --- skim the slides for anything you have not already met;
- the [recommendations](#NASEMrec) --- the table is searchable, so look up the three factors on your group's shortlist.

Mark up your sheet as you go: correct the numbers you got wrong, and note which of your three factors you now want to keep, and which you want to swap.

**Read with your own role in mind.** You will shortly be drafting as the data, analysis or reporting lead, and this is the only part of the session where you are reading rather than arguing --- so note down what you will want when it is your turn to write.

By the end of this step your group should have a **corrected sheet and a settled shortlist** --- the evidence checked, the three factors chosen. That is everything the charter needs to be built on.

#### 📊 The Factors, Together <span style="color:dimgray;">(10 minutes)</span> {#factors}

I will take us through the factors that break reproducibility, drawing on the [slides](#PartBteaching) and on the recommendations of @NAP25303. Since you have read @Baker_2016 already, this is a short synthesis rather than a walk through the paper.

Keep the three factors from the [previous step](#recall) in front of you: if something named here is not on your list, add it --- your charter is about to have to deal with it.


#### ✍️ Draft Your Charter <span style="color:dimgray;">(30 minutes)</span> {#draftcharter}

**Write it in a shared document.** Before you start, one member of each group creates a **Google Doc** (preferred, because all three of you can type in it at once) or a **Word document**, names it `Charter_Group1` or `Charter_Group2`, and saves it in our shared Google Drive at [`Reproducible_Science > Chapters > Chapter_1 > Part_B`](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1l3ZwbVjiswHWdW38wt5Hd7VxS-_uHKOG?usp=drive_link). Give it four headings --- **Definitions**, **Data**, **Analysis**, **Reporting**. Each lead writes under their own section today; the **Definitions** block is completed as homework (see the end of this step).

Keeping it in that folder is what makes the rest of the activity work: it is how the three of you draft together, how you carry on after class, and how the other group opens your charter to stress-test it.

Each lead drafts the clauses for their own section. Between you, the charter must address all three factors from the [first step](#recall), and you may consult the [recommendations table](#NASEMrec) for wording and for what others have proposed.

**Be ready to say where each clause comes from** --- a failure you saw in [Part A](#CaseStudies), a factor reported by @Baker_2016, or a recommendation from @NAP25303. A clause nobody can source is usually a habit, not a standard.

**The standard is that a clause must be checkable.** Somebody outside your group should be able to tell whether you followed it:

- ❌ *"We will document our data well."*
- ✅ *"Every dataset has a README recording who collected it, when, with what instrument, and what each column means, written before the data leave the field laptop."*

For each clause, be ready to say **what it costs** --- in time, in effort, or in freedom to change your mind later. A standard nobody can afford is a standard nobody will keep.

**You are not starting from nothing.** The box below gives each lead a set of questions to work through, one worked example to show the level of detail expected, and where to look in the course material. Aim for **two or three clauses per section** --- six to nine in total is a charter; twenty is a wish-list. The three definitions go at the top, and are written as homework once the clauses are settled.

<details id="chartertemplate">
<summary><b>🧭 Starting points for each section</b></summary>

<p><b>📜 Definitions</b> --- completed as homework, see <a href="#IntroDef">Introduction and Definitions</a> in Part A. One line each for <i>reproducible science</i>, <i>reproducibility</i> and <i>replicability</i>, in your own words. Write them <b>after</b> your clauses, not before: it is far easier to say what your standards are for once you can see what they actually are.</p>

<p><b>Everyone:</b> the four strategies in <a href="#WrapUp">Wrap-up and Future Directions</a> --- detailed protocols, laboratory notebooks, version control, and data and code repositories --- are the obvious backbone. Your charter should say something about each of them, in the section where it belongs.</p>

<p><b>📊 Data lead</b> --- see <a href="#partDM">Data Management</a> (Chapt. 5) and the data life cycle: create, process, document, preserve, share, reuse.</p>
<ul>
  <li>Where do raw data live the moment they are created, and where is the second copy?</li>
  <li>How would somebody who was not there know what each file, and each column, contains?</li>
  <li>What has to be written down <em>at the time</em> because it cannot be reconstructed later?</li>
  <li>What happens to the raw file once cleaning starts?</li>
</ul>
<p><em>Example clause:</em> "Raw data are never edited. All cleaning happens in a script, and the raw file is kept read-only."</p>

<p><b>💻 Analysis lead</b> --- see <a href="#repcode">Reproducible Code</a> (Chapt. 5).</p>
<ul>
  <li>Which decisions in an analysis get made <em>after</em> seeing the data, and which should be fixed before?</li>
  <li>If your laptop disappeared tomorrow, what would somebody need in order to re-run your analysis?</li>
  <li>How do you record which version of which software produced a given result?</li>
  <li>How does a number in your manuscript get traced back to the code that produced it?</li>
</ul>
<p><em>Example clause:</em> "Every figure and table in a manuscript is produced by code that runs from the raw data with a single command."</p>

<p><b>📢 Reporting lead</b> --- see <a href="#chap4">Open Science and CARE Principles</a> and <a href="#getpub">Getting Published</a>.</p>
<ul>
  <li>What must a reader have in order to check your central claim for themselves?</li>
  <li><em>When</em> does that become available --- at submission, at acceptance, on request, or never?</li>
  <li>How are data, code and software credited, and who is an author?</li>
  <li>What do you report when an analysis did not work, or was abandoned?</li>
</ul>
<p><em>Example clause:</em> "Data and code are deposited before submission, not after acceptance, and every software package is cited with its version."</p>

</details>

<blockquote>
📌 <b>Before Session 2:</b> finish the draft. You are not expected to leave today with a complete charter --- you are expected to leave with every section started and the hard arguments had. Each lead completes their own clauses as homework <b>in the shared document</b>, so the group arrives with <b>one agreed draft</b> rather than three sets of notes. Have it finished before the next session starts --- the other group opens it straight away.
<br><br>
<b>Then add the Definitions block at the top of the charter.</b> Three entries, <b>one line each</b>:
<ul>
  <li><b>Reproducible science</b> --- what it is, in a single sentence;</li>
  <li><b>Reproducibility</b> --- what it means to reproduce a study;</li>
  <li><b>Replicability</b> --- and how that differs.</li>
</ul>
Use the definitions you worked on in class in <a href="#IntroDef">Introduction and Definitions</a> (Part A), <b>written in your own words</b> rather than copied. As set out in the [Goal](#WhatFacBreakRep), these lines are what the rest of your charter is in service of --- and in the next session the other group will read them first, then check whether your clauses actually deliver them.
</blockquote>

#### 🔍 Stress-Test Another Team's Charter <span style="color:dimgray;">(20 minutes)</span> {#stresstest}

**Open the other group's charter** from [`Reproducible_Science > Chapters > Chapter_1 > Part_B`](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1l3ZwbVjiswHWdW38wt5Hd7VxS-_uHKOG?usp=drive_link) --- you review theirs, they review yours. Add your challenges as **comments in their document**, so they can see exactly which clause each objection lands on. Your job now is to be the sceptic:

a. **Which clause breaks first** when a deadline is three days away?
b. **Which clause is unenforceable** --- how would anyone know it had been broken?
c. **What is missing?** Look at the retracted articles and Table \@ref(tab:retractionwatch) in [Part A](#CaseStudies): would this charter have prevented those retractions?
d. **Do the clauses serve the definitions?** Read the Definitions block at the top, then the clauses below it. Does this charter actually deliver what the group says reproducible science is?

Then hand it back. **Each lead answers the challenges to their own section**, replying to the comments on their own clauses --- defend the clause, or concede and rewrite it. Both are good answers; neither is a loss. The comment thread is worth keeping: it is a record of which standards survived scrutiny and which did not.


#### ✅ Revise and Commit <span style="color:dimgray;">(15 minutes)</span> {#commitcharter}

Revise your charter in the light of the challenges, then each student states, out loud, **one clause from their own section that they will apply to their own project this semester** --- starting now, not in principle.

We will keep the charters, and they will guide the rest of the course. What you have written today is developed in [Chapt. 4 -- Open Science and CARE Principles](#chap4), in [Data Management](#partDM) and [Reproducible Code](#repcode) in Chapt. 5, and in [Chapt. 6 -- Getting Published and Peer Review](#chap6). We will return to your charter as we go: each time, you should be able to take a clause you wrote today and say how you would now actually implement it.

<blockquote>
💡 <b>Why a charter?</b> Diagnosing other people's failures is comparatively easy. Deciding what <i>your</i> group will always do --- knowing it will cost you something, and that colleagues can hold you to it --- is what a research lead actually does. That is the skill this activity is for.
</blockquote>


# Chapt. 2 -- R, R Markdown and User-Defined Functions {#chap2}
## Introduction

In this chapter, we introduce the use of **bioinformatics tools for writing and disseminating reproducible reports**, as implemented in RStudio [@RStudio]. More specifically, we will learn how to **link and execute data and code within a unified environment** (see Figure \@ref(fig:ReproScience)). 


### Aim

This chapter aims to ***equip students with the essential skills required to effectively use R Markdown for integrating text, code, figures, tables, and references into a cohesive, reproducible document***. The final output can be rendered into multiple formats—including `PDF`, `HTML`, or `Word`—to streamline the communication and sharing of research findings.

This tutorial provides students with the foundational knowledge necessary to complete their bioinformatics tutorials (**PART 2**) and individual projects (**PART 3**).

### Objectives

The chapter is divided into six parts, each with specific learning objectives:

- [**PART A:**](#partA) Learning the Basics
- [**PART B:**](#partB) Setting Your R Markdown Document
- [**PART C:**](#partC) Tables, Figures, and References  
- [**PART D:**](#partD) Advanced R Markdown Settings  
- [**PART E:**](#partE) User-Defined Functions in R  
- [**PART F:**](#partF) Interactive Tutorials  

```{r ReproScience, fig.alt="A left-to-right gradient scale from blue to gold: a blue box labeled Publication only sits at the not reproducible end, a wide middle box labeled Publication plus contains three graded levels (Data, then Data and code, then Linked and executable data and code), and a gold box labeled Full replication sits at the gold standard end.", echo=FALSE, fig.cap="The spectrum of reproducibility.", fig.show="asis", out.width = '100%'}
knitr::include_graphics("Figures/Fig1.png")
```

Files supporting this chapter are available on [Google Drive](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1Olb6huHcBfv02OxL50WEbQR-uJvkuX7O?usp=drive_link).

### Install R Markdown Software

Software and packages required to perform this tutorial are detailed below. Students should install those software and packages on their personal computers to be able to complete this course. Additional packages might need to be installed and the instructor will provide guidance on how to install those as part of the forthcoming tutorials.

- **R**: https://www.r-project.org
- **R packages**: `bookdown`, `knitr` and `R Markdown`. Use the following R command to install those packages:
```{r eval=F, tidy=TRUE}
install.packages(c("bookdown","knitr", "rmarkdown"))
```
- **RStudio**: https://www.rstudio.com/products/rstudio/download/
- **TeX**: This software is required to compile document into `pdf` format. Please install MiKTeX on Windows, MacTeX on OS X and TeXLive on Linux. **For this class, you are not requested to install this software**, which takes significant hard drive space and is harder to operate on Windows OS. 

**NOTE:** The instructor is using the following version of `RStudio`: Version 2025.05.0+496 (2025.05.0+496). If your computer is experiencing issues running the latest version of the software, you can install previous versions [here](https://docs.posit.co/previous-versions/rstudio/).

### What is RStudio?

RStudio [@RStudio] is an **integrated development environment (IDE)** that allows you to interact with R more efficiently. While similar to the standard R GUI, RStudio is significantly more user-friendly. It offers more drop-down menus, tabbed windows, and extensive customization options (see Figure \@ref(fig:IDE)). 

Detailed information on using RStudio can be found on [RStudio’s website](https://support.rstudio.com/hc/en-us/sections/200107586-Using-RStudio).

```

## PART A: Learning the Basics {#partA}

In this part, we will provide a survey of the procedures to create and render (or knitting) your first R Markdown document.

### Learning Outcomes

This tutorial provides students with the opportunity to learn how to:

- [Create and render (or "knit") your first R Markdown document](#firstMDhow)
- Understand basic Markdown syntax and conventions, including:
    + [Headers](#headers)  
    + [Inside text commenting](#comment)  
    + [Lists](#lists)  
    + [Italicizing and bolding text](#itbold) 
    + [Creating hyperlinks](#hyperlinks)  
    + [Including code chunks](#codechunkhow)
    + [Inline code](#inlinecode)  
    + [Checking spelling](#checkspell)

### Introduction to R Markdown {#IntroRMd}

Markdown is a simple formatting syntax used for authoring HTML, PDF, and Microsoft Word documents. It is implemented in the `rmarkdown` package. An R Markdown document is typically divided into three sections (see Figure \@ref(fig:RMdown)):

1. **YAML metadata section:** This section provides high-level information about the output format of the R Markdown file. The information defined here is used by the Pandoc program to format the final document (see Figure \@ref(fig:RMdown)).
2. **Main body text:** This section represents the core content of your document or publication and uses Markdown syntax.
3. **Code chunks:** This section allows you to import and analyze data, and to produce figures and tables that are directly embedded in the output document.

```{r RMdown, fig.alt="Screenshot of an R Markdown file open in the RStudio source editor, with overlaid labels marking the YAML metadata section between the triple dashes at the top, the publication core text in the middle, a shaded code chunk labeled importing data, and a second shaded chunk labeled analyze data and output figures and tables.", echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Example of an R Markdown file showing the three major sections.", fig.show="asis", out.width = '100%'}
knitr::include_graphics("Figures/Presentation_RMarkdown.png")
```

### Your First R Markdown Document {#firstMDhow}

In this section, you will learn how to create and knit your first R Markdown document.

#### Create Document

To create an R Markdown document, follow these steps in RStudio:

1. Navigate to: `File -> New File -> R Markdown...`  
2. Enter a title for your document and set the output format to `HTML` (see Figure \@ref(fig:RMdownscreen))
    - **Title:** `Chapter 2 - Part A` (This is the title of your document, not the name of your file; see below)
    - **Note:** We will knit documents to the `HTML` format, which is the default output in RStudio. If you prefer to generate a `PDF` document, you must have a version of the `TeX` program installed on your computer (see Figure \@ref(fig:RMdownscreen)).  
3. Save the `.Rmd` file by selecting: `File -> Save As...`  
    - **File name:** `Chapter_2_part_A.Rmd`  
    - **Project path:** `Reproducible_Science/Chapters/Chapter_2`  
    - **Warning:** Because the knitting process generates multiple files, you should save your `.Rmd` file in a dedicated project folder.

```{r RMdownscreen, fig.alt="Screenshot of the RStudio New R Markdown dialog box, with Document selected in the left-hand list, a Title field, a date field, HTML selected among the Default Output Format radio buttons, and Create Empty Document, OK and Cancel buttons along the bottom.", echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Snapshot of window to create an R Markdown file.", fig.show="asis", out.width = '40%', fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("Figures/Create_RMarkdown.png")
```

#### Knit Document

To knit ![](Figures/knit_2.png){alt=""} or render your R Markdown document into an HTML file, follow these steps in RStudio:

1. Click the `Knit` button (Figure \@ref(fig:RMdown)) in the top toolbar to render the document.  
2. There are several output format options; however, if you simply click the button, RStudio will automatically knit the document using the settings specified in the YAML metadata section (Figure \@ref(fig:RMdown)).  
3. The output file will be created in the same directory as your `.Rmd` file (Figure \@ref(fig:MyFirstRMfolder)). You can monitor the progress in the **R Markdown** console.  

<style>
.info {
  background-color: #e7f3fe;
  border-left: 6px solid #2196F3;
}
</style>
<div class="info">
  <p><strong>💡 Info</strong> If the knitting process fails, error messages will appear in the Render console, often indicating the line in the script where the error occurred (although this is not always the case). These messages are helpful for debugging your R Markdown document.
  </p>
</div>

```{r MyFirstRMfolder, fig.alt="Screenshot of a macOS Finder list view showing an expanded folder named Chapter_2 containing two files, Chapter_2_part_A.html and Chapter_2_part_A.Rmd.", echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Snapshot of your project folder with the knitted html document.", fig.show="asis", out.width = '100%', fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("Figures/MyFirstRMarkdown_HTML.png")
```

#### <a name="compilation"></a>How Does the Knitting Process Work?

When you knit your document, R Markdown passes the `.Rmd` file to the R *knitr* package, which executes all code chunks and generates a new Markdown (`.md`) file. This Markdown file includes both the code and its output (see Figure \@ref(fig:Rflow)).

The `.md` file created by *knitr* is then processed by the Pandoc program, which converts it into the final output format (e.g., HTML, PDF, or Word) as illustrated in Figure \@ref(fig:Rflow).

```{r Rflow, fig.alt="A left-to-right pipeline of five stages joined by arrows: an .Rmd file icon, a knitr box, an .md file icon, a pandoc box, and finally a stack of output document icons.", echo=FALSE, fig.cap="R Markdown flow.", out.width = '100%'}
knitr::include_graphics("Figures/rmarkdownflow.png")
```

**Note:** The **Cheatsheets** section also provides access to other helpful resources related to R Markdown and data manipulation. These documents will be very useful throughout this course.

### Headers {#headers}

Below is the syntax to create headers at three levels:

**Syntax:**
```{r eval=FALSE}
The "#" refers to the level of the header
# Header 1

## Header 2  

### Header 3  
```  

<div class="info">
  <p><strong>💡 Info</strong></p>
  <ul>
    <li>While Markdown headers will render correctly without blank lines, it is best practice to include blank lines both before and after headers. Doing so improves the readability of the raw Markdown and helps minimize knitting quirks. Overall, including a blank line before a header (except at the very start of a document) and after it is not strictly required, but it makes your Markdown cleaner and more consistent.</li>  </ul>
</div>

### Inside Text Commenting {#comment}

Markdown does not have a built-in syntax for adding comments within text, but you can use HTML-style comments instead:

```{r eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
# HTML syntax to comment inside text
<!-- COMMENT -->
```

This syntax is typically used to highlight areas of the text that need revision, clarification, or further work. Comments inserted this way will not be visible in the knitted document.

You can learn more about this HTML syntax on this [webpage](https://www.w3schools.com/html/html_comments.asp).

### Lists {#lists}

There are two types of lists:

- Unordered
- Ordered

#### Syntax for unordered lists

**Syntax:**
```{r eval=FALSE}
* unordered list
* item 2
  + sub-item 1
  + sub-item 2
```

**Note:** For each sub-level include two tabs to create the hierarchy.

**Output:**

* unordered list
* item 2
  + sub-item 1
  + sub-item 2

      <li>Checking your code by knitting the document</li>
    </ul>
  </p>
</div>

#### Syntax for ordered lists

**Syntax:**
```{r eval=FALSE}
1. ordered list
2. item 2
   + sub-item 1
   + sub-item 2
```

**Output:**

1. ordered list
2. item 2
   + sub-item 1
   + sub-item 2

### Italicize and Bold Words {#itbold}

The following syntax renders text in *italics*, **bold**, or ***both italics and bold***: 

```{r eval=FALSE}
#Syntax for italics
*italics*

#Syntax for bold
**bold**

#Syntax for italic and bold
***italic and bold***
```

**Output:**

- *Italic*
- **Bold**
- ***Italic and bold***

### Create Hyperlinks {#hyperlinks}

Adding hyperlinks to your documents support reproducible science and it can be easily done with the following syntax:

```{r eval=FALSE}
#Syntax to add hyperlink
[text](link)

#Example to provide hyperlink to RStudio
[RStudio](https://www.rstudio.com)
```

When knitted, the example with RStudio turns like that [RStudio](https://www.rstudio.com).

### Include Code Chunks {#codechunkhow}

One of the most exciting features of working with the R Markdown format is the ability to directly *embed* the output of R code into the compiled document (see Figure \@ref(fig:Rflow)). 

In other words, when you compile your `.Rmd` file, R Markdown will automatically execute each code chunk and inline code expression (see example below), and insert their results into the final document.

If the output is a table or a figure, you can assign a label to it (by adding metadata within the code chunk; see Part B) and refer to it later in your `PDF` or `HTML` document. This process—known as *cross-referencing*—is made possible through the `\@ref()` function, which is implemented in the R `bookdown` package.
 
#### Code Chunk

A code chunk can be easily inserted into your document using one of the following methods:

- Using the keyboard shortcut **Ctrl + Alt + I** (on macOS: **Cmd + Option + I**).
- Clicking the `Insert` button ![](Figures/insert_code_chunk.png){alt=""} in the editor toolbar.
- Typing ```{r} to open the chunk and ``` to close it.

By default, the code chunk expects R code, but you can also insert chunks for other programming languages (e.g., Bash, Python).

  background-color: #ffdddd;
  border-left: 6px solid #f44336;
}

    <ul>
      <li>Creating a code chunk in your R Markdown document that prints the message "Hello world" when you knit the document</li>
    </ul>
  </p>
</div>

#### Chunk Options

Chunk output can be customized with *knitr* options arguments set in the `{}` of a code chunk header. In the examples displayed in Figure \@ref(fig:RChunk) five arguments are used:

- `include = FALSE` prevents code and results from appearing in the finished file. R Markdown still runs the code in the chunk, and the results can be used by other chunks.
- `echo = FALSE` prevents code, but not the results from appearing in the finished file. This is a useful way to embed figures.
- `message = FALSE` prevents messages that are generated by code from appearing in the finished file.
- `warning = FALSE` prevents warnings that are generated by code from appearing in the finished.
- `fig.cap = "..."` adds a caption to graphical results.

We will delve more into chunk options in part D of chapter 2, but in the meantime please see the R Markdown Reference Guide for more details. 

```{r RChunk, fig.alt="Screenshot of RStudio split between the source editor on the left, showing an .Rmd file whose code chunks carry different options such as include equals FALSE, message and warning equals FALSE, and fig.cap, and the Viewer pane on the right showing the knitted page with a purple-to-yellow heatmap and its caption.", echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Example of code chunks.", out.width = '100%'}
knitr::include_graphics("Figures/code-1-options.png")
```

### Inline Code {#inlinecode}

Code results can also be inserted directly into the text of a `.Rmd` file by enclosing the code as follows:
```{r eval=FALSE}
# Syntax for inline code
``r 2+2`` # Please amend to include only 1 back tick
```

**Output:**
`r 2+2`

R Markdown will always:

- Display the results of inline code, but not the code.
- Apply relevant text formatting to the results.

As a result, inline output is indistinguishable from the surrounding text. 

**Warning:** Inline expressions do not take *knitr* options and is therefore less versatile. We usually use inline code to perform simple stats (e.g. 4x4; `r 4*4`)

## PART B: Setting Your R Markdown Document {#partB}

### Introduction

The **aim** of this tutorial is to develop an R Markdown document that can be used as a template to produce your reproducible reports. 

We will focus on learning how to configure your document to manage software dependencies, set global parameters for knitting, and produce appendices with software citations, package version information, and details about the operating system used to generate the reproducible report.

This tutorial provides students with the opportunity to learn how to:

### Structure of an R Markdown Document {#structRMD}

To facilitate the teaching of the learning outcomes, a roadmap of the R Markdown file (`*.Rmd`) structure is summarized in Figure \@ref(fig:RMarkdwnstrct).

To support the reproducibility of your research, we structure the R Markdown file as follows (Figure \@ref(fig:RMarkdwnstrct)):

1. The YAML metadata section (at the top of the document) must include information about your bibliography (`*.bib`) and citation style language (`*.csl`) files, both of which must be stored in the working directory.
2. Two R code chunks are provided just below the YAML metadata section:
    - [Code chunk #1]{.underline}: Installs and loads packages, and generates a `packages.bib` file (stored in the working directory).
    - [Code chunk #2]{.underline}: Sets global options for code chunks.
3. The Markdown section beneath the two R code chunks is edited to add headers for the References and Appendices sections.
4. Finally, two R code chunks are included in the Appendices section:
    - [Code chunk #3]{.underline}: Provides citations of software (relying on the output of Code chunk #1) for Appendix 1.
    - [Code chunk #4]{.underline}: Provides software version information (relying on *sessionInfo()*) for Appendix 2.

```{r RMarkdwnstrct, fig.alt="A stacked block diagram of an .Rmd file read top to bottom: a green YAML metadata block, then blue code chunks for packages and setup, a white YOUR RESEARCH block, and headings for References and Appendices followed by two further blue code chunks for software citations and package versions; arrows on the right connect four blocks to notes about declaring .bib and .csl files, loading and analyzing data, automatic formatting of references, and using packages.bib to build the software bibliography.", echo=FALSE, fig.cap = "Representation of the RMarkdown file structure taught in this class. The following colors represent the three main computing languages found in an RMarkdown document: Black: Markdown (we also sometimes use HTML), Green: YAML, and Blue: R (included in code chunks). See text for more details.", fig.show = "asis", out.width = '100%'}
knitr::include_graphics("Figures/RMarkdown_file_structure.png")
```

### YAML Metadata Section {#YAMLset}

The YAML metadata section (Figure \@ref(fig:RMarkdwnstrct)) allows users to provide arguments (referred to as *fields*) that control how an R Markdown document is converted into its final output format. In this class, we will use functions from the *knitr* [@R-knitr; @knitr2015] and *bookdown* [@R-bookdown; @bookdown2016] packages to populate this section. (Field names, as declared in the YAML metadata section, are provided in parentheses.)

1. Title (`title`)
2. Subtitle (`subtitle`)
3. Author(s) (`author`)
4. Date (`date`)
5. Output format(s) (`output`)
6. Citations link (`link-citations`)
7. Font size (`fontsize`)
8. Bibliography file(s) (`bibliography`)
9. Citation style file for journal formatting (`csl`)

The YAML code shown below generates either an `HTML` or `PDF` document (see the `output` field), includes a table of contents (see the `toc` field), and formats in-text citations and the bibliography section according to the journal style specified in the `AmJBot.csl` file (via the `csl` field). The bibliography must be stored in a `.bib` file (in this case, `Bibliography_Reproducible_Science_2.bib`) placed at the root of your working directory.

```{r YAML, eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE}
--- 
title: "Your title"
subtitle: "Your subtitle"
author: "Your name"
date: "`r Sys.Date()`"
output:
  bookdown::html_document2: 
    toc: TRUE
  bookdown::pdf_document2:
    toc: TRUE
link-citations: yes
fontsize: 12pt
bibliography: Bibliography_Reproducible_Science_2.bib 
csl: AmJBot.csl
---
```

#### Step-by-Step Procedure

Follow these steps to set up your YAML metadata section (also see Figure \@ref(fig:RMarkdwnstrct)):

1. Make sure you have created a document following the approach described [here](#creatRMDfile)
2. Copy the following files, available on [Google Drive](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1JFjKmb0JHm96UfimO8SJLq33hE1JRu5v?usp=drive_link), into your project folder:  
    + `Bibliography_Reproducible_Science_2.bib`  
    + `AmJBot.csl`  
3. Replace your YAML metadata section (at the top of your R Markdown document) with the code as shown in the [section above](#YAMLset)
4. Knit your document and inspect the output file. Read this [section](#knitmore) to get more details on the knitting procedure.  

<div class="info">
  <p><strong>💡 Info</strong></p>
  <ul>
    <li><b>Warning:</b> The `.bib` and `.csl` files must be stored in the same working directory as your `.Rmd` file.</li>
    <li><b><code>R</code> functions in the YAML metadata section:</b> This can be done using inline R code syntax. For example, use <code>Sys.Date()</code> to automatically add the current date to the output document.</li>
    <li><b>Bibliography files:</b> You can use multiple bibliography files by specifying them like this: <code>bibliography: [file1.bib, file2.bib]</code>.</li>
    <li><b>Omitting parameters in the YAML metadata section:</b> You can omit parameters by commenting them out with a <code>#</code> at the beginning of the line (equivalent to commenting).</li>
    <li><b>More information:</b> To learn more about YAML and its use in R Markdown, visit this 
      <a href="https://zsmith27.github.io/rmarkdown_crash-course/lesson-4-yaml-headers.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">website</a>.
    </li>
  </ul>
</div>

#### Knitting Procedure {#knitmore}

Since you have declared two output formats in the YAML metadata section, and both are specific to `bookdown` functions, you need to select which format you want to use to compile your document. To do this, click the drop-down menu to the left of the `Knit` button (see Figure \@ref(fig:knitout)).

To ensure that `bookdown` functions are applied correctly, make sure to select one of the following options (see Figure \@ref(fig:knitout)):

- `Knit to html_document2`
- `Knit to pdf_document2`

knitr::include_graphics("Figures/knit_drop_down.png")
```

### Install R Dependencies and Load Packages {#loadRreq}

#### Introduction

It is best practice to **add an R code chunk** directly below the YAML metadata section **to automatically install and load the required R packages**.

This approach offers two key benefits that support the reproducibility of your research:

1. It ensures that all dependencies needed to produce your document are installed and available (see Figure \@ref(fig:RMarkdwnstrct)).  
2. It allows you to automatically generate a citation file for all R packages used in your report (see [below](#citfileRpkg)).

  <p><strong>💡 Disclaimer</strong></p>
  <ul>
    <li><b>Warning:</b> The code provided in this section will install the following <code>R</code> packages on your computer: "knitr", "rmarkdown", "bookdown", "formattable", "kableExtra", "dplyr", "magrittr", "prettydoc", "htmltools", "knitcitations", "bibtex", "devtools".</li>
    <li><b>More on the <code>R</code> packages:</b> These packages are required to produce your reproducible reports in RStudio. All of them are available on <a href="https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">CRAN</a>, the official repository for <code>R</code>.</li>

You can do this by following <a href="https://docs.posit.co/ide/user/ide/guide/environments/r/packages.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">this procedure</a>.</li>

  </ul>
</div>

#### Step-by-Step Procedure

1. Insert an R code chunk ![](Figures/insert_code_chunk.png){alt=""} directly below your YAML metadata section (see Figure \@ref(fig:RMarkdwnstrct)).
2. Name the code chunk `packages` and set the chunk options as follows (see Figure \@ref(fig:packageschunkfig)):
   + `echo = FALSE`  
   + `warning = FALSE`  
   + `include = FALSE`
```{r packageschunkfig, fig.alt="Close-up of a single R Markdown chunk header that opens with three backticks and reads r packages, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, include=FALSE, followed by the closing backticks on the next line.", echo=FALSE, fig.cap = "This is how your packages R code chunk should look like at this stage of the procedure.", fig.show = "asis", out.width = '100%'}
knitr::include_graphics("Figures/packages_code_chunk_options.png")
```
3. Copy the following code into your R code chunk (Figure \@ref(fig:packageschunkfig)) to install and load the packages required to produce your report:

```{r eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE, tidy = FALSE}
###~~~
# Load R packages
###~~~
#Create a vector w/ the required R packages
# --> If you have a new dependency, don't forget to add it in this vector
pkg <- c("knitr", "rmarkdown", "bookdown", "formattable", "kableExtra", "dplyr", "magrittr", "prettydoc", "htmltools", "knitcitations", "bibtex", "devtools")

##~~~
#2. Check if pkg are already installed on your computer
##~~~
print("Check if packages are installed")
#This line outputs a list of packages that are not installed
new.pkg <- pkg[!(pkg %in% installed.packages())]

##~~~
#3. Install missing packages
##~~~
# Use an if/else statement to check whether packages have to be installed
# WARNING: If your target R package is not deposited on CRAN then you need to adjust code/function
if(length(new.pkg) > 0){
  print(paste("Install missing package(s):", new.pkg, sep=' '))
  install.packages(new.pkg, dependencies = TRUE)
}else{
  print("All packages are already installed!")
}

##~~~
#4. Load all required packages
##~~~
print("Load packages and return status")
#Here we use the sapply() function to require all the packages
# To know more about the function type ?sapply() in R console
sapply(pkg, require, character.only = TRUE)
```

4. Review the R code to ensure you understand what it does and why
5. Knit your document and inspect the output file

### Generate a Citation File of R Packages Used {#citfileRpkg}

#### Introduction

I do not know about you, but I often struggle to properly cite R packages in my publications. Fortunately, R provides a built-in function to help with this. If you want to retrieve the citation for an R package, you can use the base R function `citation()`.

For example, the citation for the *knitr* package can be obtained as follows:

```{r cit, eval=T, echo=TRUE}
#Generate citation for knitr
# Type this code directly in the Console
citation("knitr")
```

If you want to generate those citation entries in BibTeX format, you can pass the object returned by `citation()` to `toBibtex()` as follows:

```{r cit2, eval=T, echo=TRUE}
#Generate citation for knitr in BibTex format
#Note that there is no citation identifiers. Those will be automatically generated in our next code. 
utils::toBibtex(utils::citation("knitr"))
```

<div class="info">
  <p><strong>💡 Info</strong></p>
  <ul>
    <li>
      Note that both <code>citation()</code> and <code>toBibtex()</code> are functions in the 
      <i>utils</i> R package.
    </li>
    <li>
      <strong>To make sure that you are calling the right R function</strong>, you can add the package 
      name in front of the function, followed by <code>::</code>. In this example, the code is as follows: 
      <code>utils::toBibtex(utils::citation("knitr"))</code>.
    </li>
  </ul>
</div>

#### Step-by-Step Procedure

Here, you will edit the `packages` code chunk to output a `.bib` file containing references for all R packages used to generate your document. This file will be included in the appendix 1 presented in the next section.

This can be done by **adding the following code at the end of your `packages` R code chunk**:

```{r cit3, eval=F, echo=TRUE}
#Generate BibTex citation file for all loaded R packages used to produce report
# Notice the syntax used here to call the function
knitr::write_bib(.packages(), file = 'packages.bib')
```

The `.packages()` function returns *invisibly* the names of all packages loaded in the current R session (to see the output, use `.packages(all.available = TRUE)`). This ensures that all packages used in your code will have their citation entries written to the `.bib` file.

Finally, to be able to cite these references (see [Citation identifier](#citationidentifier)) in your text, you need to edit the [YAML metadata section](#YAMLset). See [Appendix 1] for a full list of references associated with the R packages used to generate this report.

    <li>Knitting your document and inspecting your project folder to observe the creation of a new file entitled <code>packages.bib</code>.</li>
  </ul>
</div>

### Generate Appendix with Citations of Used R Packages {#appendixRpkg}

Although a References section will be provided at the end of your document to cite in-text references (see [References] and Figure \@ref(fig:RMarkdwnstrct)), it is useful to create a customized appendix listing citations for all R packages used to conduct the research, as shown in [Appendix 1]. 

Here, we will learn the procedure to assemble such an appendix.

#### Step-by-Step Procedure

1. Add a level-1 header at the end of your document titled "References".
2. Include the appendices after the References section (see Figure \@ref(fig:RMarkdwnstrct)) by following the steps below:  
   + Insert `<div id="refs"></div>` as shown below. This ensures that the appendices (or any other material) appear *after* the References section.  
     (See [this resource](https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown-cookbook/bibliography.html#include-appendix-after-bibliography) for more details.)
```{r eval=FALSE}
# References

<div id="refs"></div>

# (APPENDIX) Appendices {-}

# Appendix 1

Citations of all R packages used to generate this report.
```
3. Insert an R code chunk ![](Figures/insert_code_chunk.png){alt=""} directly below `# Appendix 1` to read and print the citations saved in `packages.bib`. Use the following code:
```{r generateBibliography1, eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE, warning = FALSE, message=FALSE}
###
#Load R package
###
library("knitcitations")

###
#Process and print citations in packages.bib
###
# Clear all bibliography that could be in the cash
cleanbib()
# Set pandoc as the default output option for bib
options("citation_format" = "pandoc")
# Read and print bib from file
read.bibtex(file = "packages.bib")
``` 
4. Edit your R code chunk options as follows to correctly print the references:  
   `{r generateBibliography, results = "asis", echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}`
5. Knit your document to check that it produces the correct output (see [Knitting procedure]). Refer to [Appendix 1] to see an example of the expected result.

---

### Generate Appendix with R Package Versions and Operating System {#appendixRverOS}

In addition to citing R packages, you may also want to provide detailed information about the R package versions and operating system used (see Figure \@ref(fig:RMarkdwnstrct)).

In R, the simplest — yet highly useful and important — way to document your environment is to include the output of `sessionInfo()` (or `devtools::session_info()`). Among other details, this output shows all loaded packages and their versions from the R session used to run your analysis.

Providing this information allows others to reproduce your work more reliably, as they will know exactly which packages, versions, and operating system were used to execute the code.

For example, here is the output of `sessionInfo()` showing the R version and packages I used to create this document:

```{r eval=T, echo=T}
# Collect Information About the Current R Session
sessionInfo()
```

#### Step-by-Step Procedure

I have also used the approach described above to add this information in [Appendix 2]. This can be done as follows:

1. Edit your document to add the following text below Appendix 1.
```{r eval = FALSE}
# Appendix 2

Version information about R, the operating system (OS) and attached or R loaded packages. This appendix was generated using `sessionInfo()`.
```
2. Then, add an R code chunk ![](Figures/insert_code_chunk.png){alt=""} and set its options as follows to correctly print the content:  
   `{r sessionInfo, eval = TRUE, echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}`
3. Copy this code in your code chunk:
```{r eval=F, echo=T, warning = FALSE, message=FALSE}
#Load and provide all packages and versions
sessionInfo()
```
4. Knit your document to check that it produces the correct output.

---

### All Set — You’re Good to Go!

You have now set up your R Markdown environment and are ready to start populating it! This means you can begin inserting your text and additional code chunks directly below the `packages` code chunk.

The [References] section marks the end of the main body of your document. If you wish to add appendices, do so under [Appendix 2]. Note that appendices will be labeled differently from the main sections of the document.

## PART C: Tables, Figures and References {#partC}

### Introduction

The **aim** of this tutorial is to provide students with the expertise to generate reproducible reports using *bookdown* [@R-bookdown; @bookdown2016] and related R packages (see [Appendix 1] for a full list). Unlike the functions implemented in the R *rmarkdown* package [@rmarkdown2018, which is better suited for generating `PDF` reproducible reports], *bookdown* allows the use of **one** unified set of functions to generate both `HTML` and `PDF` documents.

In addition, the same approach and functions are used to **process tables and figures, as well as to cross-reference them in the main body of the text**. This tutorial will also cover **how to cite references in the text, automatically generate a references section, and format citations according to journal styles**.

### Learning Outcomes

This tutorial provides students with the opportunity to learn how to:

- [Insert tables in an R Markdown document](#inserttable)
- [Insert figures in an R Markdown document](#insertfigure)
- [Cross-reference tables and figures in the text](#crossrefTabFig)
- [Cite references in the text](#bib)
- [Generate a References section](#refsection)
- [Format citations according to journal style](#cslForm)

### Insert Tables {#inserttable}

This tutorial introduces key concepts related to table creation in R Markdown, specifically the following:

- Creating a table based on R code  
- Assigning a table caption  
- Providing a unique label to the R code chunk for cross-referencing in the text  
- Displaying the table in the document  

More details on this topic will be provided in Chapter 9.

In this section, you will learn the R Markdown syntax and R code needed to replicate the grading scale presented in the syllabus (see Table \@ref(tab:tabgrades)).
 
```{r tabgrades, echo=F, fig.align='center'}
#Create a data.frame w/ grading scale
grades <- data.frame(Percentage = c("100-98","97.9-93", "92.9-90", "89.9-88", "87.9-83", "82.9-80", "79.9-78", "77.9-73", "72.9-70", "69.9-68", "67.9-60", "59.9-0"), Grade = c("A+","A","A-","B+","B","B-","C+","C","C-","D+","D","F"))
#Plot table
knitr::kable(grades, caption = "Grading scale applied in this class.", format = "html") %>% kable_styling(c("striped","scale_down"))
```

2. Add a first-level header titled `Tables` below the `packages`code chunk.  
3. Insert an R code chunk under your header by clicking the `Insert` button ![](Figures/insert.png){alt=""} in the editor toolbar.  
4. Copy and paste the following R code into your code chunk:

###

knitr::kable(grades, caption = "Grading scale applied in this class.", format = "html") %>% kableExtra::kable_styling(c("striped","scale_down"))

5. Edit the R code chunk options line by adding the following argument (**Note:** each argument should be separated by a comma):

Click the play icon in the top-right corner of the code chunk to execute the code and return its output directly in the R Markdown document without knitting.", fig.show = "asis", out.width = '100%'}

<div class="danger">
  <p><strong>💡 Is something missing?</strong></p>
  <ul>
    <li><strong>Challenge:</strong> Scrutinize the code provided in this section to determine how the table caption is created.</li>

#### Double "Table" in Caption <span style="color:dimgray;">(10 minutes)</span>

Several students have encountered an issue with duplicate table labels in the caption. The instructor did a web search and found a possible solution to help debug the issue:

- **Problem:** When using `kableExtra::kbl()` or `knitr::kable()` in combination with `kableExtra` functions, you might see a caption like "Table Table X: Your Caption".
- **Solution:** Specify the `format` argument in `knitr::kable()` (e.g., `format = "html"`), or use `kableExtra::kbl()` directly, which automatically handles the format. This prevents `kableExtra` from re-interpreting a markdown table as a new table and adding an extra "Table" prefix.

In our case, we could try editing the code as follows (two options):

```{r tabgrades3, eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE}
###
# Load package (for testing)
###
library(dplyr)

###
# Create a data.frame w/ grading scale
###
grades <- data.frame(Percentage = c("100-98","97.9-93", "92.9-90", "89.9-88", "87.9-83", "82.9-80", "79.9-78", "77.9-73", "72.9-70", "69.9-68", "67.9-60", "59.9-0"), Grade = c("A+","A","A-","B+","B","B-","C+","C","C-","D+","D","F"))

###
# Plot table and add caption
###

# Option 1
knitr::kable(grades, caption = "Grading scale applied in this class.", format = "html") %>% kableExtra::kable_styling(c("striped","scale_down"))

# Option 2
kableExtra::kbl(grades, caption = "Grading scale applied in this class.") %>%
kableExtra::kable_styling(c("striped","scale_down"))
```

The instructor encourages students to test the options proposed above in their own documents and determine whether they resolve the issue.

### Cross-reference Tables and Figures in the Text {#crossrefTabFig}

Cross-referencing tables and figures in the main body of your R Markdown document can easily be done by using the `\@ref()` function implemented in  the *bookdown* package (see Figure \@ref(fig:RMarkdwnstrct)). 

#### General Syntax

The general syntax is as follows:

```{r synt, eval=F}
# Cross-referencing tables in main body of text
Table \@ref(tab:code_chunk_ID)

# Cross-referencing figures in main body of text
Figure \@ref(fig:code_chunk_ID)
```

<div class="info">
  <p><strong>💡 More Info on the Syntax</strong></p>
  <ul>
    <li>It is worth mentioning that you need to manually add <code>Table</code> or <code>Figure</code> in front of <code>\@ref(tab:code_chunk_ID)</code> or <code>\@ref(fig:code_chunk_ID)</code>. This design allows the user to choose how tables and figures are referenced in the text. Journals often have distinct formatting styles, which must be followed during submission.</li>
  </ul>
</div>

#### Step-by-Step Procedure <span style="color:dimgray;">(10 minutes)</span>

1. To cross-reference your table (labeled `tabgrades`) in the text, follow these steps:
    - Type the following sentence below your `Tables` header:  
      `The grading scale presented in the syllabus is available in Table \@ref(tab:tabgrades).`
    - Knit your document using the `Knit` button ![](Figures/knit_2.png){alt=""} in the editor toolbar (see Figure \@ref(fig:knitout)) to inspect the output and verify that the syntax and code are working correctly.

2. To cross-reference your figure (labeled `cars`) in the text, follow these steps:
    - Type the following sentence below your `Figures` header:  
      `The plot of the cars data is available in Figure \@ref(fig:cars).`
    - Knit your document using the `Knit` button ![](Figures/knit_2.png){alt=""} in the editor toolbar (see Figure \@ref(fig:knitout)) to inspect the output and verify that the syntax and code are working correctly.

### Cite References in the Text {#bib}

#### Introduction

In this section, we will cover the following topics before delving into the practical implementation of citing references in your R Markdown document:

- [The Bibliography File](#bibFile)
- [The BibTeX Format](#BibTexFormat)
- [Citation Identifier](#citationidentifier)

##### The Bibliography File {#bibFile}

Pandoc can automatically generate citations in your text and a References section following a specific journal style (see Figure \@ref(fig:RMarkdwnstrct)). To use this feature, you need to declare a bibliography file in the [YAML metadata section] under the `bibliography:` field.

In this course, we are working with bibliography files formatted using the [`BibTeX`](#BibTexFormat) format. Other formats can also be used — please see this [resource](https://rmarkdown.rstudio.com/authoring_bibliographies_and_citations.html) for more details.

Most journals allow citations to be downloaded in `BibTeX` format, but if this feature is not available, you can convert citation formats using online services (e.g., EndNote to BibTeX: https://www.bruot.org/ris2bib/).

##### The BibTeX Format {#BibTexFormat}

**BibTeX is a reference management tool commonly used** in conjunction with LaTeX (a Markup language) **to format lists of references** in scientific documents. It allows users to maintain a bibliographic database (`.bib` file) and cite references in a consistent and automated way.

Each entry in a `.bib` file follows this general structure:

Please find below an example of a reference formatted in `BibTeX` format:

```{r eval = FALSE}
@entrytype{citationIndentifier,
  field1 = {value1},
  field2 = {value2},
  ...
}
```

<div class="info">
  <p><strong>💡 Info on BibTeX format</strong></p>
  <ul>
    <li><strong><code>&#64;entrytype</code>:</strong> Type of reference (e.g., <code>&#64;article, &#64;book, &#64;inproceedings</code>).</li>
    <li><strong>citationIdentifier:</strong> Unique ID used to cite the entry in your R Markdown document.</li>
    <li><strong>fields:</strong> Key-value pairs with bibliographic information (e.g., author, title, year).</li>
  </ul>
</div>

Here is an example associated with @Baker_2016:

```{r eval = FALSE}
# Example of BibTex format for Baker (2016) published in Nature
@Article{Baker_2016,
  doi = {10.1038/533452a},
  url = {https://doi.org/10.1038/533452a},
  year = {2016},
  month = {may},
  publisher = {Springer Nature},
  volume = {533},
  number = {7604},
  pages = {452--454},
  author = {Monya Baker},
  title = {1,500 scientists lift the lid on reproducibility},
  journal = {Nature},
}
```

##### Citation Identifier {#citationidentifier}

The unique citation identifier of a reference (`Baker_2016` in the example above) is set by the user in the `BibTeX` citation file (see the first lines in the examples provided above). This identifier is used to refer to the publication in the R Markdown document and also enables citing references and generating the References section.

#### Step-by-Step Procedures

In this section, we will cover the following topics to implement the tools for references citing in your R Markdown document:

- [Steps to Complete Before Citing References in Your Text](#stepsbeforeciting)
- [Cite References in Your Text](#citerefintext)

##### Steps to Complete Before Citing References in Your Text {#stepsbeforeciting}  

1. Save all your `BibTeX`-formatted references in a bibliography text file, and make sure to add the `.bib` or `.bibtex` extension.  
2. Place the bibliography file in your project folder (alongside your `.Rmd` file).  
3. Declare the name of your bibliography file in the [YAML metadata section] under the `bibliography:` field.  
4. References formatted in the `BibTeX` format are available in the following file:  
    + `Bibliography_Reproducible_Science_2.bib`

###### Challenge <span style="color:dimgray;">(5 minutes)</span>

<div class="danger">
  <p><strong>💡 Download a Citation in BibTeX Format</strong></p>
  <ul>
    <li>Visit this <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/botlinnean/box083" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">webpage</a>.</li>
    <li>Locate the <code>Cite</code> icon and download a citation in <code>.bibtex</code> format.</li>
    <li>Open the <code>.bibtex</code> file in a text editor and inspect its contents.</li>
    <li>What is the unique citation identifier of this article?</li>
  </ul>
</div>

##### Cite References in Your Text {#citerefintext}

We will examine the syntax for citing references, either as parenthetical citations or in-text citations.

- [Parenthetical Citation:](#parentcitation) The entire citation appears in parentheses, usually at the end of a sentence or clause.  
- [In-Text Citation:](#intextcitation) The author's name is part of the sentence, and the citation appears naturally in the flow of the text.

###### Parenthetical Citation {#parentcitation}

In this case, citations are placed inside square brackets (`[]`) (usually at the end of a sentence or clause) and separated by semicolons. Each citation must include a key composed of `@` followed by the citation identifier (as stored in the `BibTeX` file).

Please find below some examples on citation syntax:

```{r eval=FALSE}
#Syntax
Blah blah [see @Baker_2016, pp. 33-35; also @Smith2016, ch. 1].
Blah blah [@Baker_2016; @Smith2016].
```

Once knitted (using the ![Knit](Figures/knit_2.png) button), the citation syntax is rendered as:

Blah blah [see @Baker_2016, pp. 33–35; also @Smith2016, ch. 1].

Blah blah [@Baker_2016; @Smith2016].

A minus sign (`-`) before the `@` symbol will suppress the author's name in the citation. This is useful when the author is already mentioned in the text:
```{r eval=FALSE}
#Syntax
Baker says blah blah [-@Baker_2016].
```

Once knitted, the citation is rendered as:

Baker says blah blah [-@Baker_2016].

###### In-Text Citation {#intextcitation}

In this case, in-text citations can be rendered with the following syntax:
```{r eval=FALSE}
#Syntax
@Baker_2016 says blah.
@Baker_2016 [p. 1] says blah.
```

Once knitted, the citation is rendered as:

@Baker_2016 says blah.

@Baker_2016 [p. 1] says blah.

    <li>Write a sentence citing &#64;Baker_2016 using parenthetical citation syntax.</li>
    <li>Write a sentence citing &#64;Baker_2016 using in-text citation syntax.</li>
  </ul>
</div>

Upon knitting, a References section will automatically be generated and inserted at the end of your document (see Figure \@ref(fig:RMarkdwnstrct)). 

We recommend adding a level-1 "References" header immediately after the final paragraph of the document, as shown below:

```{r eval=FALSE}
last paragraph...

```

The bibliography will be inserted after this header (please see the [References] section of this tutorial for more details).
